fatal_errors: The hypothesis substitutes a refractory Nb-Mo-Ta-W-V-type alloy for the target equimolar Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Ti system, so it does not reconstruct the material or its Ti-controlled FCC/BCC constitution.

The proposed ordered-BCC/disordered-BCC or BCC/FCC dual phase is speculative: the cited refractory-alloy evidence instead reports either two BCC solutions in milled powder, oxygen-derived TiO after SPS, or decomposition into Laves phases.
SPS at 900-1000 degrees C is asserted to densify the refractory alloy while retaining sub-50 nm grains, but the cited refractory studies do not establish this low-temperature process window.
The falsification experiment mainly tests temperature stability and intermetallic formation; it does not distinguish Hall-Petch/dislocation strengthening from simple solid-solution strengthening.
The stated starting condition is a cast alloy, whereas the intervention requires mechanical alloying of elemental powders.
explanation: The response captures the broad MA/HEBM plus SPS strategy and correctly invokes repeated welding/fracture, milling-induced defects, grain-boundary strengthening, and rapid consolidation. Its 900-1000 degrees C processing range and hardness above 600 Hv also overlap the target qualitatively. However, it changes the chemistry, extends milling from 1-6 h to more than 40 h, changes the ball-to-powder ratio and SPS heating rate, and does not recover the target 83% FCC/17% BCC phase balance. Predicted yield strength above 2000 MPa and ductility above 10% conflict with the target result of 1238 MPa yield stress and limited ductility/intergranular fracture. Evidence discipline is weak because empirical VEC and atomic-size criteria for general BCC formation do not demonstrate a stable dual-phase, intermetallic-free refractory alloy, and the cited SPS studies actually show TiO or Laves formation. A discriminating test should independently vary grain size while holding composition and phase fractions constant, then test Hall-Petch scaling against a coarse-grained control; the proposed 950 versus 1200 degrees C comparison changes grain size, phase constitution, and precipitation simultaneously.
